newsitem.title: UK: Koreans embark on UK chemicals shopping trip.
newsitem.headline: Koreans embark on UK chemicals shopping trip.

text.p: Specialty chemicals, technology and joint ventures are at the top of a shopping list for representatives of South Korea's chemical industry in Britain this week, UK trade officials said on Monday.

Some 20 members of the Korea Specialty Chemical Industry Association KSCIA) will be looking at opportunities to use British expertise to strengthen their own production of specialty products, particularly in organic chemicals and pharmaceutical intermediates.

Alan Twist, who is spending two years on secondment to the UK Department of Trade and Industry from Imperial Chemical Industries Plc, told Reuters these were areas "where Britain is strong and Korea is not so strong".

"Korea is strong in the building blocks of the chemical industry, but medium-sized companies are keen to go into niche specialty areas," said Twist, who is working for the DTI to boost links between the Korean and British chemical industries.

KSCIA executive director Ik-Ha Choi said that despite strong growth in chemical production, which has risen by more than 10 percent a year for the past decade, Korea was "struggling for the invention of new materials."
He said the industry's goal was to boost spending on domestic research and development to reduce reliance on imported specialty chemicals.

"There seem to be some opportunities for British companies who can supply the materials, intermediates and the technology required for the Korean chemical companies' research and development activities," he said.
Britain currently enjoys a trade surplus with Korea in chemicals, with exports of 147 million stg in 1996 and imports of 100 million stg.
However Korea is fast catching Britain up. In 1995 Korea's total chemical output stood at $40 billion compared with Britain's $60 billion.
But ICI's Twist said he did not believe Britain was in danger of selling its leadership to the Koreans, as it had in other industries.
"The British are aware of the value of their technology and are skilled at selling it pretty dear," said Twist.
He said chemicals were not in the same league as cars, where the Koreans have built themselves into a major international force, far eclipsing Britain.
"Chemistry is different from that. It is about pure creativity rather than a developmental process," said Twist, who spent five years working for ICI in Korea.

"Many Koreans agree that their education system does not stimulate creativity or blue sky research. In Britain we have always been strong in creative skills. Koreans are very strong in operations skills," he added.

The main focus of the week-long trip will be a visit to the Chemspec exhibition in Manchester on Wednesday at which Britain's specialty chemicals industry displays its wares. The Koreans will also be meeting representatives from chemical companies in the north-east of England, and visiting Zeneca Group Plc's new pharmaceutical intermediates plant at Huddersfield on Wednesday.
Twist said there were hopes that the Koreans might be tempted to set up their own operations in Britain, following in the footsteps of electronics giants like Samsung Group and LG International.
The Korean party will visit Samsung's showpiece electronics plant on Teesside, north-east England, on Tuesday.
